steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction to a robotics/vision paper presenting 2DPnP, a PnP algorithm for estimating the pose of a camera constrained to move in a plane. Introduce the PnP problem and existing solvers, explain the trouble with coplanar points, and motivate our 2D approach.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- The PnP problem: definition and setup
- Exact solvers for small n; overconstrained case and reprojection error
- Iterative vs non-iterative solutions
- Planar point configurations and ambiguity
- Existing mitigations and their limits
- Our setting (2D camera motion) and the 2DPnP algorithm

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- PnP problem
  - find pose of perspective camera from correspondences image points <-> world points
  - given n 3D points \textbf{p}_{i}, projections \textbf{q}_{i} on image plane
  - want rigid transformation matrix R camera frame -> world frame, for each 1\leq i\leq n: (equation)
  - z_{i} depth factors; known intrinsics remap \textbf{q}_{i} to normalized perspective camera
- Exact / overconstrained
  - n=3 exactly solvable -> P3P algorithms (cite); also P4P, P5P (cite)
  - want all correspondences to reduce noise -> overconstrained, approximate solution
  - minimize reprojection error: sum of squared distances between \textbf{q}_{i} and projection of \textbf{p}_{i} onto predicted image plane (equation)
  - not necessarily pixels, because of normalization
- Iterative vs non-iterative
  - reprojection error: simple geometric criterion, common in iterative PnP; alternatives e.g. object-space error of Lu et al. (cite)
  - EPnP (Lepetit et al.): four weighted control points, O(n) (cite)
  - OPnP (Zheng et al.): analytically minimizes algebraic error by solving polynomial system (cite)
  - at time of publication: state of the art mostly non-iterative polynomial solvers; iterative like Lu et al.'s LHM still competitive
  - many non-iterative solvers (cite) end with iterative refinement; Gauss-Newton suffices
- Planar configurations
  - PnP great for many correspondences spread widely in 3D; many suboptimal when coplanar
  - EPnP has special planar case; coplanarity allows homography-based solvers, e.g. IPPE of Collins and Bartoli (cite), higher precision
  - planar = ambiguity even for specialized solvers: images from multiple camera positions very similar / indistinguishable with noise
  - worse at low resolution, long distance, plane almost parallel to image plane
  - illustrate: square fiducial marker, corners used for pose (figure)
- Mitigations
  - well-known problem (cite), many methods
  - iterative initialized with last known pose -> stability, but can get persistently stuck in wrong pose
  - IPPE etc. compute all possible solutions, pick best or return all
  - fuse with other sensor info (cite)
  - only a facet of deeper issue of imprecision for planar configs
- Our setting
  - camera constrained to 2D movement (e.g. wheeled robot); PnP used with environmental landmarks or fiducials
  - full 3D pose loses information; 3D poses must be projected onto plane of movement
  - algorithm using 2D constraint from start: better accuracy (error stays in plane of motion instead of 'escaping' into disallowed poses); performance gain from lower-dimensional search space
  - 2DPnP: simple, meets criteria; approximate solution via combined geometric + algebraic methods, then iteratively minimize reprojection error

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The perspective- n -point (PnP) problem is about finding the pose of a perspective camera using correspondences between points in the image and points in world coordinates. We have n 3D points \textbf{p}_{i} and their corresponding projections onto the image plane, \textbf{q}_{i}. We want to find a rigid transformation matrix R from the camera frame to the world frame so that, for each 1\leq i\leq n:

Here the z_{i} are the depth factors, and we use the known camera intrinsics to remap the \textbf{q}_{i} so they model the normalized perspective camera. In the case n=3 this can be solved exactly, which gives the class of P3P algorithms as in. P4P and P5P algorithms have been developed in the same way too. However, we want to use all the correspondences we have in order to reduce the impact of noise, and then the problem is overconstrained and we can only get an approximate solution. One way is to minimize the reprojection error, which is the sum of squared distances between each \textbf{q}_{i} and the projection of its \textbf{p}_{i} onto the predicted image plane. This is:

Because we normalized the \textbf{q}_{i}, this is not necessarily a distance in pixels. Minimizing the reprojection error is a simple geometric criterion that is commonly used in iterative PnP solutions, but there are many other errors, like the object-space error of Lu et al.. There are also non-iterative solutions. One is the EPnP algorithm by Lepetit et al., which uses four weighted control points to get the time complexity down to O(n). Another is the OPnP algorithm of Zheng et al., which minimizes an algebraic error analytically by solving a system of polynomial equations. At the time of publication, the state-of-the-art PnP solutions were mostly non-iterative polynomial system solvers, but iterative solutions such as Lu et al.'s LHM are still competitive. Also, many non-iterative solvers, including the two above, have an iterative phase at the end that refines the predicted pose (a simple optimization algorithm like Gauss-Newton is enough for this).

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The perspective- n -point (PnP) problem is about finding the pose of a perspective camera using correspondences between points in the image and points in world coordinates. We have n 3D points \textbf{p}_{i} and their corresponding projections onto the image plane, \textbf{q}_{i}. We want to find a rigid transformation matrix R from the camera frame to the world frame so that, for each 1\leq i\leq n:

Here the z_{i} are the depth factors, and we use the known camera intrinsics to remap the \textbf{q}_{i} so they model the normalized perspective camera. In the case n=3 this can be solved exactly, which gives the class of P3P algorithms as in. P4P and P5P algorithms have been developed in the same way too. However, we want to use all the correspondences we have in order to reduce the impact of noise, and then the problem is overconstrained and we can only get an approximate solution. One way is to minimize the reprojection error, which is the sum of squared distances between each \textbf{q}_{i} and the projection of its \textbf{p}_{i} onto the predicted image plane. This is:

Because we normalized the \textbf{q}_{i}, this is not necessarily a distance in pixels. Minimizing the reprojection error is a simple geometric criterion that is commonly used in iterative PnP solutions, but there are many other errors, like the object-space error of Lu et al.. There are also non-iterative solutions. One is the EPnP algorithm by Lepetit et al., which uses four weighted control points to get the time complexity down to O(n). Another is the OPnP algorithm of Zheng et al., which minimizes an algebraic error analytically by solving a system of polynomial equations. At the time of publication, the state-of-the-art PnP solutions were mostly non-iterative polynomial system solvers, but iterative solutions such as Lu et al.'s LHM are still competitive. Also, many non-iterative solvers, including the two above, have an iterative phase at the end that refines the predicted pose (a simple optimization algorithm like Gauss-Newton is enough for this).

PnP algorithms are very accurate when there are many correspondences spread widely in 3D space, but many of them behave suboptimally when the points are coplanar. Some algorithms like EPnP have a special case for planar configurations. Assuming coplanarity also lets us use homography-based solvers such as the IPPE solver of Collins and Bartoli, which use the unique structure of the problem to get higher precision. But planar configurations are a challege even for the specialized solvers, because they can produce ambiguity: the images seen from multiple camera positions can be very similar, or even indistinguishable when there is noise. The problem gets worse at low resolutions and long distances, and when the plane containing the points is almost parallel to the image plane. We show the possible ambiguity with a square fiducial marker, whose corners are often used for pose estimation:

This problem is well-known, and many methods have been proposed to deal with it. For example, iterative algorithms can be initialized with the last known pose to make them more stable (but this means they can become persistently stuck in the wrong pose). Some algorithms, like IPPE, try to compute all possible solutions and then either select the best fit or return the solutions to the user. The outputs of existing algorithms can also be fused with other sensor information as in. However robust these solutions are, they only solve a facet of the deeper issue of imprecision for planar configurations.

In this paper we look at the case where the camera is constrained to two-dimensional movement (for example, when it is mounted to a wheeled robot). In this case PnP algorithms are commonly used to estimate pose from environmental landmarks or fiducials. But estimating the full 3D pose loses valuable information here, because the returned 3D poses have to be projected onto the plane of movement. An algorithm that takes the 2D constraint into account from the start would probably be more accurate, since it can account for error while staying in the plane of motion instead of 'escaping' into disallowed poses. It could also perform better because the dimensionality of the search space is reduced. We derive an example of such an algorithm, called 2DPnP, which succeeds in these criteria even though it is simple. Our algorithm finds an approximate solution with combined geometric and algebraic methods, and then uses it as a starting point to iteratively minimize the reprojection error.

steps.text:
The perspective- n -point (PnP) problem asks us to find the pose of a perspective camera using correspondences between image points and points in world coordinates. We are given n 3D points \textbf{p}_{i} and their corresponding projections onto the image plane, \textbf{q}_{i}. We wish to find a rigid transformation matrix R from the camera frame to the world frame such that, for each 1\leq i\leq n:

Here, the z_{i} are the depth factors, and we use known camera intrinsics to remap the \textbf{q}_{i} so that they model the normalized perspective camera. This is exactly solvable in the case n=3, which gives rise to the class of P3P algorithms as in [1]. P4P and P5P algorithms have also been developed along these lines [2]. However, using all available correspondences is desirable to reduce the impact of noise, in which case the problem is overconstrained and we must settle for an approximate solution. One approach is to minimize the reprojection error, the sum of squared distances between each \textbf{q}_{i} and the projection of its \textbf{p}_{i} onto the predicted image plane. This is given by:

Note that, due to our normalization of the \textbf{q}_{i}, this does not necessarily measure the distance in pixels. Minimization of the reprojection error is a simple, geometric criterion commonly used in iterative PnP solutions; there are many alternative errors, such as the object-space error of Lu et al. [3]. Non-iterative solutions also exist, such as the EPnP algorithm of Lepetit et al., which uses four weighted control points to reduce time complexity to O(n) [4], or the OPnP algorithm of Zheng et al., which analytically minimizes an algebraic error by solving a system of polynomial equations [5]. At the time of publication, state-of-the-art PnP solutions were mostly non-iterative polynomial system solvers, but iterative solutions such as Lu et al.'s LHM remain competitive, and many non-iterative solvers, including [4,5], have an iterative phase at the end to refine the predicted pose (a simple optimization algorithm like Gauss-Newton suffices for this purpose).

PnP algorithms have excellent accuracy for large numbers of correspondences spread widely in 3D space, but many behave suboptimally when the points are coplanar. Some algorithms such as EPnP include a special case for planar configurations, and assuming coplanarity allows the use of homography-based solvers such as the IPPE solver of Collins and Bartoli [6], which take advantage of the problem's unique structure to achieve higher precision. However, planar configurations present a challege even for specialized solvers because they can produce ambiguity: the images seen from multiple camera positions can be very similar (or even indistinguishable in the presence of noise). The problem gets worse at low resolutions and long distances, or when the plane containing the points is almost parallel to the image plane. We illustrate the possible ambiguity with a square fiducial marker, whose corners are often used for pose estimation:

This problem is well-known [7,8], and many methods have been proposed to mitigate it. For instance, iterative algorithms can be initialized with the last known pose to improve stability (although this means they can become persistently stuck in the wrong pose). Some algorithms, such as IPPE, attempt to compute all possible solutions, then either select the best fit or return the solutions to the user. The outputs of existing algorithms can also be fused with other sensor information as in [9]. However, robust as these solutions are, they solve only a facet of the deeper issue of imprecision for planar configurations.

This paper deals with the case of a camera constrained to two-dimensional movement (for instance, one mounted to a wheeled robot). Here, PnP algorithms are commonly used to estimate pose from environmental landmarks or fiducials. However, estimating the full 3D pose loses valuable information in this situation, since the returned 3D poses must be projected onto the plane of movement. An algorithm that takes the 2D constraint into account in the first place would likely be more accurate, because it can account for error while remaining in the plane of motion instead of 'escaping' into disallowed poses. Performance improvements could also come from the reduced dimensionality of the search space. We derive an example of such an algorithm, called 2DPnP, which succeeds in these criteria despite its simplicity. Our algorithm finds an approximate solution using combined geometric and algebraic methods, and uses it as a starting point to iteratively minimize the reprojection error.
